questions.question: The sliding-window strategy is "indiscriminate by time". What is its deep defect?
options: Every eviction requires an extra model call
It evicts by recency, not importance, so task anchors (constraints set at the start) are exactly what tends to be dropped
It cannot retain the most recent few turns
It automatically shrinks the window limit
questions.explanation: See the "The sliding window: simplest, and best at losing anchors" section: the deep defect is indifference — it evicts by time, not by importance, and task anchors usually appear at the start of a conversation, which is exactly the position evicted first.

questions.question: What does the key discipline "compression is not eviction" in summary compression mean?
options: After each compression, the entire old history is cleared
Constraints, commitments, and anomalous events must be written verbatim into the summary body, not left to the model's loose recollection
A summary may only be one paragraph long
Summary generation must block the current request
questions.explanation: See the "Summary compression: one generation buys a big block of budget" section: the key discipline is that compression is not eviction — constraints, commitments, and anomalous events must be written into the summary verbatim; numbers, dates, and proper names must be quoted as-is.

questions.question: Among the three memory strategies, which has the highest fidelity and naturally supports cross-session memory?
options: External storage (database / vector store, retrieved and injected on demand)
questions.explanation: See the "The trade-off table and the privacy boundary" section: fidelity — sliding window is lowest, summary is middle, external storage is highest; external storage naturally supports cross-session memory (a preference noticed today is still there tomorrow).
